summary: For ages 10–11 (NGSS 5-PS3-1), help children trace the energy in an animal's food back, link by link, to the Sun using a built model (flow chart/diagram). Plants capture light energy to make food; animals eat plants (or animals that ate plants); so the energy in any meal originally came from sunlight. Children then connect that food energy to its uses — body repair, growth, movement, and keeping warm (LS1.C) — and distinguish one-way energy flow from matter cycling. Keep it at the energy-flow level; defer photosynthesis/respiration chemistry to later.
misconceptions: Thinking animals (or their food) make their own energy, rather than the energy tracing back to the sun via plants.
Believing only plants 'use' the sun and animals are disconnected from it, missing that eaten plants pass the sun's energy along.
Assuming energy is recycled around a food chain like matter, rather than flowing one way and being used up.
Confusing energy with matter/food itself, rather than seeing energy as what the food carries.
Thinking the sun gives animals energy directly (like warmth) rather than through the food chain.

activities.title: Build and run a trace-the-energy-to-the-Sun model
steps: Assemble a food chain by placing organisms in order, e.g. Sun → grass → rabbit → fox (and later a different chain such as Sun → algae → fish → seal).

Choose the top animal eating its meal, then trace the energy's source BACKWARDS down the chain (the energy itself flowed forwards, from the Sun to the animal): from the food, back to the organism that ate the plant, back to the plant that captured sunlight, all the way to the Sun.
State in your own words where the energy in that meal originally came from.
Route the arriving food energy into what a body spends it on by sorting it into repair, growth, movement, and keeping warm.
Rebuild with a different chain and check that the trace-back always ends at the Sun.
activities.insight: In food chains like these, the energy in an animal's food can be traced link by link back to sunlight captured by a plant or alga; energy flows one way from the Sun and is spent (largely as heat), not recycled around the chain like matter.

activities.title: Reveal-the-link flow diagram with a myth-buster
steps: Work along a Sun → plant → animal → animal flow diagram, revealing at each link how the energy moved and where the meal's energy came from.
Open a 'does a fox (carnivore) really get energy from the Sun?' prompt and explain the reasoning.
Name the four uses of food energy (repair, growth, movement, warmth) from a callout.
activities.insight: Even a meat-eater's energy traces back through its prey and the plants to the Sun; the immediate food is one step, not the origin.

activities.title: Order, match, and choose to consolidate the trace-back
steps: Put the links of an energy chain in order starting from the Sun.
Match each energy use (repair, growth, movement, warmth) to an everyday example.
Choose where the energy in a fox's food originally came from, rejecting the tempting 'animals make their own energy' option.
activities.insight: The energy in everyday food traces back to the Sun, and that energy is spent on specific body functions.

activities.title: Trace your own lunch to the Sun on paper
steps: Draw a flow chart of something you ate today, tracing it back through each organism to the Sun.
Label the plant that captured the sunlight and draw a one-way energy arrow from the Sun along the chain.
Write one sentence saying what your body will use that food energy for.
activities.insight: The same trace-back applies to real meals: the energy in your lunch was once sunlight, and your body spends it on repair, growth, movement, and warmth.

activities.title: Socratic 'and before that?' trace-back with a scientist
steps: Take a meal and, with a questioning partner or scientist persona, answer 'and where did that energy come from?' at each link until you reach the Sun.
Explain why the chain stops at the Sun and not earlier.
Explain why the grass's energy comes from sunlight rather than the soil.
activities.insight: Repeatedly asking 'and before that?' exposes that, for everyday meals, every link's energy ultimately comes from the Sun through plants or algae.

checkQuestion: A lion eats a zebra, and the zebra eats grass. Where did the energy in the lion's body originally come from? A friend says 'from the meat' — can you trace it further back than that, all the way to its true source?
checkAnswer: Ultimately the Sun. Plants (the grass) capture light energy by photosynthesis to make food; the zebra gets energy by eating the grass; the lion gets it by eating the zebra. So the energy in the lion started as sunlight and passed along the chain — the meat is just one step, not the origin.
